Hi... yes, it’s good to meet you too. Thank you for seeing me. 

Well, it’s... it’s actually a bit difficult to articulate, which is frustrating for me because, well, I’m a social worker. I was an avid journaler, too. I have stacks and stacks of notebooks at home filled with thoughts and reflections. 

But lately... I don't know, I just look at my journals and feel absolutely nothing. I don't take pleasure in any of it anymore, not even my work, which really scares me given the populations I serve. I’m mostly just... I'm just moving through my obligations. I wake up, I go to work because I have to, I pay my bills, I eat because it's time to eat, but that spark, that drive to actually participate in my life and connect with the world... it's just gone so very quiet. Well, it’s... it’s been a gradual process, but if I really sit down and trace it back, I’d say this whole shift—this change in how I’m thinking, how I’m working, how I’m connecting with people—has been going on for about eight months.

She had a fall, and it just wasn't safe for her to live alone anymore, so we cleared out the guest room and moved her in. And, you know, as a social worker, I thought, "I handle crises all day, I can manage this transition." But having her in our space... it really changed the dynamic of the household. It wasn't just the physical space, it was the emotional space, too. Suddenly, there were all these new routines, new worries, doctor's appointments to coordinate, dietary restrictions to keep track of. 

And I think, at first, I just chalked it up to being tired. You know, caregiver burnout is a very real thing, and I see it in my clients all the time. So I told myself, "Oh, you're just adjusting, you're just exhausted, give it time." But the fatigue never lifted. It just morphed into this... this profound emptiness. The eight months just kind of slipped by, and I kept waiting to bounce back, to find my footing again once we got into a rhythm with my aunt, but instead, I just kept retreating further and further inward. So, yes, about eight months now of just... existing, really.

Well, that's... that's the tricky part, isn't it? Because on the surface, yes, it makes perfect sense to draw that line. Stress is a massive catalyst, obviously. Well, that's... that's the interesting thing about all this, and honestly, it's a distinction I've been trying to parse out in my own head for months now. Because if you ask me if I feel depressed—like, classically depressed, the way we usually define it clinically with the profound sadness, the tearfulness, that heavy, aching feeling in your chest—I'd have to say no. It's like the emotional bandwidth I used to have has just been completely dialed down to zero. I can look at a situation that should make me feel sad, or a situation that should make me feel happy, and I just feel... neutral. Blank. 

So, no, I haven't been walking around for the last eight months feeling depressed or down in the dumps. It's almost like I wish I did feel sad, because at least sadness is a feeling, you know? At least sadness means you're still connecting with something, that something still matters enough to make you hurt. But this is just a void. It's an emptiness. It's not depression, it's just... nothing. And that nothingness has been there pretty much every day, all day, for this entire eight-month stretch. It's exhausting in its own strange way, just being so completely devoid of any emotional resonance, but no, I wouldn't call it feeling depressed.

Well, no. No, I haven't. And honestly, that kind of ties right back into what I was just trying to explain about the emptiness. Because if you really break down what worry actually is... it requires energy, doesn't it? It requires a certain level of emotional investment in how things are going to turn out. The thought just kind of lands there and sits, and I don't spin out into those "what if" scenarios at all. It's like my brain just refuses to project into the future to find things to stress about. 

It's actually been very hard on my husband, I think, because he'll be stressed about something and looking for a sounding board, looking for me to share that burden with him like I always used to, and I just can't match his urgency. I just look at him and say, well, we'll figure it out, but without any real feeling behind it. So, no, no excessive worrying. Just that same... pervasive, heavy quiet where the worry used to be.

And outside of work, I was always doing something—I went to Vinyasa yoga three times a week, I’d spend my Saturday afternoons just wandering through different art galleries downtown, looking for new exhibits. I was an avid journaler, too. I have stacks and stacks of notebooks at home filled with thoughts and reflections. \n\nBut lately... I don't take pleasure in any of it anymore, not even my work, which really scares me given the populations I serve. I’m mostly just... I'm just moving through my obligations. I wake up, I go to work because I have to, I pay my bills, I eat because it's time to eat, but that spark, that drive to actually participate in my life and connect with the world... it's just gone so very quiet. My appetite? No, no, I wouldn't say it's changed. I mean, I'm still eating my normal amounts. 

It’s funny you ask that, because my husband and I were actually just discussing the grocery budget the other day, and I realized my eating habits are probably the one thing that has remained completely static through all of this. Tired? Well, I know I just said a moment ago that I don't wake up feeling refreshed, but I really need to be clear about what I mean by that, because it’s not—I’m not actually tired. I'm not experiencing fatigue or low physical energy. Not at all.

It's really more like... well, it’s like having a car with a completely full tank of gas, but the ignition switch is just gone. The fuel is there. The energy is there. I have all the physical capacity in the world to do things, I just don't have the... the spark to initiate them. That drive we were talking about earlier. I just sit there in that quiet space because I have no internal reason to move, not because I lack the energy to do so.

Thinking about death... no. No, not at all. 

It really just ties right back into what I was just saying about those questions on the risk assessments. Death is... well, death is a very heavy, philosophically dense concept, isn't it? When people think a lot about death—and I see this all the time with my substance abuse clients, or the ones dealing with severe, complicated grief—they're usually doing it because they're terrified of it, or they're obsessed with the legacy they're leaving behind, or they're just hyper-fixated on the fragility of everything. Trouble making decisions? No... no, actually, it’s quite the opposite. I haven't had any trouble with everyday decisions at all. 

It’s interesting you ask that, because in my line of work, you see decision paralysis all the time. Clients come in, especially those with severe anxiety or major depressive disorder, and they can't even decide what to put on in the morning. They agonize over every little choice because they’re terrified of making the wrong one, or they just feel so utterly overwhelmed by the cognitive load of it all. I know exactly what that looks like on an assessment, I see people sitting in my office completely immobilized by the thought of choosing between two entirely mundane options.

But for me, because I’m existing in this... this very flat, neutral space we've been talking about, decisions are incredibly simple. You see, to struggle with a decision, you usually have to have a preference. You have to care about the outcome. You have to weigh how one choice will make you feel versus another choice. And since I don't really feel strongly about anything right now, I don't have to weigh anything. The friction is completely gone. 

Take dinner, for example. My husband will come into the living room and ask, "Do you want chicken or pasta tonight?" Before, I might have thought about what we had yesterday, or what I was craving, or what kind of wine we had open. Now? I just say the first one he offered. "Chicken." Or I'll just say, "Whatever you'd prefer." And I truly mean it. It’s entirely mechanical. There’s no agonizing, no going back and forth. 

It’s the exact same at the clinic. When I'm doing an intake or referring a client to a specific program, I just look at the criteria, look at their presentation, and make the clinical match. A to B. It’s purely logistical. I don't sit there at my desk second-guessing myself or worrying if I made the absolute perfect choice. I just do it. Same with taking Buster out—I take him on the exact same route on our walk every single morning because it’s the standard route. I don't stand at the corner of our street debating whether we should go through the park or down the avenue today. I just turn left because left is the route.

So, no, everyday decisions aren't a problem at all. If anything, the complete lack of emotional investment makes them faster. I just do what's required or what's most efficient and move on to the next thing without a second thought.

No, no, I haven't had any thoughts like that. \n\nI know that’s a standard question—we ask it all the time during intake assessments at the clinic, it’s right there on the risk assessment forms, usually right after asking about hopelessness or despair. And I know why you have to ask it, because when someone describes this profound lack of motivation, this total absence of joy or connection to their daily life, the logical clinical leap is to assume they must be profoundly depressed and contemplating whether life is even worth continuing. It’s a very common trajectory for many of the people I see professionally. They lose their spark, and then they start wondering what the point of it all is, and then they start having those dark thoughts.\n\nBut for me, it’s completely different. It’s almost... well, it’s almost entirely devoid of that kind of existential dread. I don't sit in my living room, staring at the wall, thinking that life is meaningless or that I'd be better off not being here. The concept of life being \"worth living\" implies a sort of value judgment, a weighing of the pros and cons of existence, and as I was saying about the guilt, I'm just not operating in a space where I'm making those kinds of evaluations right now. \n\nI'm not in pain. That's the thing my husband really struggles to grasp. He sees me so detached, so indifferent to the things we used to enjoy—like our weekend trips to the coast, or even just sitting on the patio with a glass of wine—and he assumes I must be suffering terribly inside. He’ll ask me, \"Are you in a dark place? Are you having bad thoughts?\" And I have to explain to him, over and over, that it's not dark. It's not light, either. It's just... neutral. It's a flatline. \n\nTo have thoughts that life isn't worth living, you have to feel a sense of anguish, or a desperate desire to escape from something intolerable. But my current state isn't intolerable to me. It's just empty. I wake up, I take Buster for his walk, I go to the clinic, I listen to my clients, I come home, I eat dinner. I go through the motions of living without any internal friction. I don't feel a desire to end it, just as I don't feel a burning passion to engage with it. I'm just here, existing, day by day. \n\nSo, no, I haven't had any suicidal ideation, no thoughts of death, no feeling that life is a burden I want to put down. It's just... happening around me, and I'm present for it, even if I'm not really participating in it the way I used to.\n\nTask:\n- CONFIRMED: symptoms clearly present or strongly implied by the patient's words.\n- DENIED: symptoms the patient explicitly says they do NOT have\n  (e.g. \"No\", \"I don't\", \"I haven't\", \"never\").\n- Do NOT speculate.
